utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, General. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. I hear you all too well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, I want to go back to -- to begin with, I want to go back to the end of your testimony in your examination-in-chief, and that's in regard to your association with the SDS party. At transcript page 32815, you said that the SDS or its leaders had no influence whatsoever on your work, although you did have certain contacts with them, and at 32904, you said in response to a question from Judge Kwon on another matter, you said, "I was perceived as being a member of the Serbian Democratic Party," but you said that the only party you were a member of was the League of Communists. So in that regard, I'd like to show you a document and ask you a question. It's 65 ter number 06264. And the document is the transcript of the 37th session of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Supreme Defence Council dated, as you see here, 7 June 1995 on the cover page, but if we go over -- and that should be at e-court -- thank you. That's the agenda for the 37th session. If we go over to page 3 in English. And to my recollection, it's the same page in B/C/S. The meeting was held on 13 June 1995. Now, the attendees at this meeting with President Lilic, President Milosevic, President Bulatovic, and General Momcilo Perisic who was chief of the VJ General Staff, among others. Now, if we could go over to English page 31 of this document and B/C/S page 22, please. Now, the context of this discussion that you see here is that your army, the VRS, had put forward 12 generals for their promotion to be verified, including some members of the Main Staff, and you were one of them. And here General Perisic says: "We do not propose Dragomir Milosevic, who is commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and who is also an SDS member." So, General, it seems that General Perisic completely contradicts your assertion to Judge Kwon when you say the only party you were a member of was the League of Communists, does he not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I haven't fully understood your question. However, I hope I understood the gist of it, although there may be grounds for some additional questions in that regard. First of all, I cannot deny what Mr. Perisic said, because up until this moment, I wasn't aware of what he had said. It is now that I encounter this indication clearly showing that he was unaware of the situation. It is my impression that he tended to use certain arguments against my promotion, and he could only rely on the fact that I was a SDS member, which wouldn't -- well, there seems to be a precondition that if I were a member, I couldn't be promoted, and the other way round. So he compared some things that I don't believe to have been useful, and still he had to say something to the council at this session. I can see what it reads, but I deny that. I was never a member of the SDS, and that is what I can confirm. As for his words, I dispute them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So nevertheless, you've acknowledged that you had contacts with the SDS leaders and, in fact, General, in 1996, you wrote to General Mladic, and you said at 65 ter number 09139, in a letter dated 19 May that year, you said at page 2 of the English translation: "People from the inner circle of the VRS Main Staff told me that I was an SDS general, a politician's general, and a Chetnik general." At page 4, the second paragraph, you wrote: "All people ever seem to say about me was, 'He's an SDS general, and he's in cahoots with Karadzic.'" So it appears even on the basis of your own correspondence that your links with the SDS were rather pronounced?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I think it would be only fair if that could be shown to the general and he can have a chance look at these references before he answers the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh I'm sorry, I omitted to give the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I omitted to give the B/C/S paragraph and page reference numbers. If I can have your indulgence for one second, Your Honour. If we can go over to the last -- ah, no. I see the proper reference down at the bottom of the B/C/S page on the screen in front of us, and that's the third paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while he's reading that, just so that we don't lose track, with respect to 65 ter 06264, is that going to be tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't see a need. And now perhaps we could go over to the next page in B/C/S for the general. And there should be the page thereafter. Apologies. Your indulgence for a moment. It seems that we might not have all pages uploaded in B/C/S. I apologise for having misspoken. We did have the correct page on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, having had a chance to look at the pages --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Having had a chance to look at the paragraphs I've referred to, would you be able to answer my question, which was: It appears that even on the basis of your own correspondence that your links with the SDS were rather pronounced, does it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite the other way around. This does not indicate that my ties with the SDS were such that this would corroborate their existence. On the contrary. Throughout the letter, I was trying to make a statement opposing such views. You asked me about it, and yet you assert that I had acknowledged my contacts with the SDS. That kind of approach to this matter, which implies that I had conceded to having contact with them, is something that I cannot adopt, and I can't provide answers in that context. It is only logical and natural that at the time I had to have had contact with people but not with -- well, when it comes to issues such as the activities of the SDS, that was not it. As you call my acknowledgement, it wasn't an acknowledgement. It was a mere statement that I was in contact. I couldn't deny that. That is what life dictated. One needed to have contacts with people in order for certain arrangements to be made. However, that deny -- did not imply getting involved in politics. Such contacts were of different nature. That was the first thing. Next, I see this conversation with Mladic here. I would suggest to you -- or, actually, I would propose to answer the following way --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General. General, let's finish off with the question that I raised with you initially, and that was about your contacts with the SDS. Now, you've just told us that you had contacts and you weren't -- you weren't about to deny that, and did that include general contacts with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me about Dr. Karadzic, that's a separate issue. The issue before, however, was of my supposed acknowledgement of contacts with the SDS. Dr. Karadzic was not the SDS itself. My statement that I did have contacts includes what I have already said, and yet you now want me to continue discussing my contacts with Mr. Karadzic in the same vein. However, as regards my contacts with him, I will gladly answer when you put that question. I don't read that question in your questions thus far. I don't know how you include -- how you are trying to introduce that through the back door.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I take it from the answer that you've given that you did have contact with Dr. Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. And we'll come to explore that over the course of your cross-examination. And we'll come back to this document again later in your cross-examination. Now, General, in your testimony in chief at transcript page 32815, Dr. Karadzic asked you whether the civil authorities of Republika Srpska interfered in purely military matters, and you said you never experienced that from any person or structure of the government or through activities carried on by the cabinet or the Presidency. "We never had an opportunity to meet, but when we did meet, we never discussed combat activities to be carried out by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and politics never influenced the military situation." So as you've just said, you did meet; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's a yes or no answer, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards this variant of providing answers, I reject this method. I would much prefer if the method used to arrive at what I have to say would be a better one. There is a better way. I don't want anyone to draw such conclusions. See, you had contacts. Then this automatically implies certain arrangements about the system of command and control in the corps. When I said we had contacts, as regards the incident when there was a rift between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mladic, at the time I went with Mr. Cedo Sladoje because I wanted to establish some kind of contact regarding that rift because it concerned a decision made by the president of the republic to remove Mladic. If that was the contact discussed here, then I can't deny it. Of course there were contacts, but in situations when it had nothing to do with managing any combat activities. If I had occasion to visit Mr. Karadzic, it was when Mr. Stanic arrived, when he was dealing with the issue of UNPROFOR and the problems pertaining to them. Mr. Karadzic ordered that I be there in order to tell Mr. Stanic, "Here is the man who will work with you on dealing with this problem." I include that in my contacts with him. I was there. I saw two people, and in my book that's a contact, but not in the light that you are trying to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll get this back on track in a minute, but I just want to follow-up something that you've referred to in your testimony, and you talk about the occasion when and Cedo Sladoje went to go and see Dr. Karadzic, referring to a rift between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mladic. Now, you talked about that with Judge Kwon during the course of your testimony in chief, and Judge Kwon asked you some questions about the nature of the conduct of General Mladic. He asked you whether or not General Mladic wanted to be independent and not controlled by a superior body and whether your answers on that subject meant that General Mladic was disobedient or defiant to his Supreme Commander. Now, General, you said on that day that you couldn't say whether he ignored orders or declined orders because you didn't know, and you weren't aware of the details of any conflict between the two people. You were only discussing your general impression. So are -- if that was your general impression in your testimony in chief, maybe we better get to the bottom of this right now. To be perfectly clear, because you weren't in your testimony in chief, you've not ever seen or heard of Mladic ever disobeying an order from Dr. Karadzic, have you? Never. And that, General, is a yes or no question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am trying to answer the best way possible in my view to obtain the right information. If I said yes or no, I'm afraid your impression would not be the right one. If I was engaged to the full concerning the situation and combat activities, which included the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the 1st Corps of the army of BH, then that was my main preoccupation. Being engaged in such a large area, I never had an opportunity to see both of them in the same area to be able to see what it was that they actually had a conflict over. That was one thing. Another thing, I never attended any Assembly sessions of the RS Assembly. I do know that the -- such sessions were held in different locations, and I do know that basically all of the generals were there. However, I did not attend a single one. Whatever misunderstandings there may have been, whatever discussions there may have been in regard of command and control could have taken place in such situations, and yet it could have been in situations where only the two of them were present or some of their associates. However, I was not there. I couldn't see that. I couldn't realise or pinpoint what their misunderstanding or conflict was. Since I was in no situation to see it, I cannot speculate. Obviously there was a misunderstanding, and I have to be so free as to say that I could see something was wrong. Now, to what extent that was or who initiated it, that's something I don't know. I think my assertion should be enough for you, which for the time figures as the only one. I have no other -- I have no other explanations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we just go back to my question then. It's correct, then, that you've never seen or heard of General Mladic ever disobeying an order from Dr. Karadzic, have you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's correct. If I didn't see it, how could I confirm it? It doesn't mean that I'm saying that there was no recalcitrance, but I'd rather not go into it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've just said that you didn't go to Assembly sessions.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But I'd like to tell you what General Mladic, your commander, said about the nature of the army's relationship with the civilian authorities at the 50th Assembly session of the RS Assembly, and that was on April 6, 1995, and the transcript of that is P970. The relevant page -- actually, what I'll do, General, is I'll start with something that General Milovanovic, your army's deputy commander and the Chief of Staff, said at that Assembly session. I'll start at page 191 in English and page 162 in B/C/S. And there General Milovanovic said in response to a speech by Dr. Karadzic: "I don't want to comment on the speech delivered by the Supreme Commander. I'm not entitled to it. Yet I can claim again that the Main Staff never had the intention nor does it now to place itself above the state. No state where the military are in power is long lived, even where a putsch had taken place, where the army did it, it was always with the promise of bringing back a civilian government. The army, which didn't observe this, lost both the state and army. It's not up to the army to lead the state but the state to lead the army." And then if we go over to page 344 in English of this document and page 303 in B/C/S, there's a series of discussions that follow the quote I've just read to you. General Mladic himself speaks in response to and addressing Dr. Karadzic, and he says to Dr. Karadzic: "I wish to tell you, you have no idea how much I understand what a difficult role you, in particular, have, and every other man in a high position has." And then if we go over to the paragraph that follows, he says to

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "President, you don't have more competent and more honest people in Republika Srpska who could give you a better, more honest and more competent assessment of the army than your officers. I have nothing to hide from you. It's not my army. It's more yours than mine. But most of all, it's the army of the people and the state." Now, General, based on this, it seems to me that your impression of what you described as a rift actually reflects your lack of understanding of the situation, doesn't it, because Mladic here in April 1995, before an audience of the members of the Assembly, generals from the Main Staff of your army, Dr. Karadzic himself, and other members of the Supreme Command affirms he's a committed officer dedicated in service to Dr. Karadzic and his people, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you expect of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I expect you to answer my questions, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course you expect that, but I don't know in what sense. Why should I try to say something now in terms of see how he put it nicely. As to those statements, issues, and his words in that particular place at that particular time is not something that I'm going to judge. I'm not going to take the role of a man who will say this is right and this is wrong. These are issues that I have no contact with, I have no connection to, apart from seeing that these are written on the paper. I have no other answer but to say that this is not my comment, this is not my opinion, and it shouldn't be expected of me to confirm the veracity of this or otherwise. What is written here is apparent, but nobody should expect of me to confirm other people's ideas, words, utterances, or variations in their public appearances, and this is something that I cannot dwell on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine. We'll move on then. Let's go back to the situation that I put to you or the reference in your testimony in chief that I put to you at the beginning of your cross-examination where you said when you met -- when you said, "I never experienced from any person or structure of the government, either through any activities carried on by the cabinet or Presidency --" pardon me. I'll rephrase it. Where you said in respect of the government, the cabinet, or the Presidency that you never had an opportunity to meet, but when you did meet you never discussed combat activities to be carried out by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and politics didn't interest -- or influence the military situation. And I want to know you another document. That's P4925, and it's entitled "Amendment to Directive 6," and it's issued by Dr. Karadzic on 12 December 1993. Now, I think we'll probably for you, General, have to enlarge the copy in your language on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'm particularly interested in paragraph 2 at the bottom of the page. Thank you. Now, this is a directive, General, that says -- or a directive to by 21 December, 1993, when Geneva negotiations are resumed, to improve the SRK's tactical position - and if we can go over to the next page, please - by, among other things, at paragraph 2, 2(a) by among other things seizing Zuc and Mojmilo features to ensure the most favourable position for dividing the town of Sarajevo. So this document, General, is a directive ordering operations specifically timed to improve your corps' tactical position by the time political discussions resume. So isn't this actually a perfect example of how politics influence and, in fact, dictate the military situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not familiar personally with this directive at all, and in connection with such ideas or directives, this is something completely new to me apart from being able now to read it. And this reference concerning improving the situation in the theatre of operations that we discussed so far, the Sarajevo theatre, I cannot assess this in terms of saying that this is not significant. It is. It indicates that the organs of government want to create a situation which would be more favourable to them and to make the life of the people living in that area easier, living in the area where there are conflicting parties, because if you have some certain features, if you hold certain features, this is important for the defence of the area and the territory that you'd already seized, that you already have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're saying that you're not familiar with the document or you're not familiar with the operation that it directs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this is 1993, isn't it. As you know very well -- yeah. Yeah. Well, I was there. Yes, I'm -- I was made aware of that, of that action being carried out, those activities concerning the feature Zuc, but I did not take part personally in that, because General Galic commanded the corps at the time. It was none of my business to monitor closely at that situation apart from me being at the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I'm sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I read the transcript you referred to, i.e., transcript page 32815 -- I'm sorry, 32815. The question asked by Mr. Karadzic to the witness was related to the influence by the civilian authorities -- civilian authorities and especially the SDS or its leaders. I don't think that question also related to the president himself, the Supreme Commander, and I don't think the witness ever denied the role of Karadzic, the president, with respect to military affairs. Could you put more directly your question to the witness with -- as regards this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment while I look again at the transcript, please, Your Honours. Yes. And perhaps I've come about it in a cumbersome way. The question relates to, as I read it, the general's assertion that with regard to the government, the cabinet, or the Presidency, that they never had an opportunity to meet, and when they did, they never discussed combat activities to be carried out by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And I'd like to go directly to that in my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, you've just said that you were made aware of this operation being carried out, and it's true, isn't it, that you were made aware of this operation because you were part of the high level discussion in Belgrade on 13 and 14 December 1993, where the operation was planned, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct. I did attend in my capacity as a person -- well, I did not command the corps at the time, apart from the corps commander who wanted me to tag along because of possible better assessing what was to come going forward, and maybe as his first associate and expert co-worker. I was there just to attend. I did not take part in the discussion. I did not take part in putting forward any proposals, and I did not initiate any matters concerning what was to unfold later.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, at that meeting, from the Presidency, from the members of the Presidency of the republic of Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina were Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: From your army General Mladic, General Milovanovic, General Djukic, General Miletic, General Maric, and Colonel Salapura, in addition to yourself and General Galic; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm for certain people, because I cannot recall whether Salapura was there or not, whether Miletic was there or not. I cannot recall that. As for the others that you mentioned, yes, I do recall, and I know that they were there. In my previous responses to you, it slipped my mind to tell you that Mladic was the initiator of all these things. He particularly tried to go through President Milosevic to create an impression that there was a need for such a combat action to be carried out. I now can see that this is going -- this is interpreted in hindsight as the President's initiative or his proposal, but I do recall Mladic's stance at that meeting. It is true, however, that Milovanovic held a slightly different position in terms of that he needed more time for preparations. He didn't claim that taking such action would be unnecessary. And this is as far as I know about these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And from the cabinet, the RS cabinet, or the government, Mico Stanisic was also there, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember President Slobodan Milosevic, General Perisic, Jovica Stanisic, and Frenki Simatovic taking part?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do recall President Milosevic and Mr. Perisic. As for Stanisic, I -- I didn't know that person. And since there were no introduction at the meeting, he may have been there, but I did not pay any attention to him, because he represented a service which does not want to flaunt its presence around. I cannot confirm Mr. Simatovic either. So I cannot confirm that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. Now, in your testimony in chief, you said that when you met, you never discussed combat activities to be carried out by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, at 32815. The specific purpose, General, of this meeting was to plan, to discuss and plan, the operation to be carried out in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you do not want to hear the right answer, and you're trying to lead me to give you an answer which is favourable to your cause. I wasn't the driver of that meeting, the initiator. I wasn't somebody who was meeting President Karadzic pursuant to the need to resolve those issues concerning combat actions. When I said I did not meet him on these matters, I mean I did not meet him separately or meet him in terms of my capacity and my function concerning those activities pertaining to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. There was no such separate meeting, or there was no meeting between me and President Karadzic alone. For instance, if there were briefings, military briefings, such briefings would be attended by President Karadzic. In my eyes, this was not a discussion on how combat activities should be carried out. Such briefings were used to discuss many matters, and president would receive reports on what was going on within the Republika Srpska Army throughout the territory. I would not treat that as a meeting concerning the issue that you want me to give you an answer about concerning the Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In transcript, I don't believe that the "vojna savjetovanja" should not be translated as "military briefings." Military briefings are daily operational activities, and "vojna savjetovanja" has a different -- completely different meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I can't help that. Probably you may ask the general about the meaning or what it was like. General, I don't remember the term, but if you could assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if it went to military conferences or military meetings, I presume that this is what I am supposed to elucidate upon. Of course, this is not a briefing or a short meeting that would be for the purposes of exchanging brief instructions or orders. Military conferences concerned military matters. There were -- there were usually annual conferences. There was no prescribed frequency, and they would discuss military matters and developments. This would be a review of the preceding year in terms of military matters and in connection with the aforesaid to take stance on improvements or new solutions or correction of certain deficiencies for the future period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, General, you're referring to the annual -- the briefings on combat readiness which took place at the end of January and the beginning of February every year, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not discussing that, no. I said that military conferences or military consultations were places where the Main Staff would find it necessary to invite the president of the republic to make a review of the preceding year. It doesn't have to be in January, because we're not in peacetime. We could not plan certain slots for that meeting. It took place when it could, when the circumstances were right, when arrangements for everybody to be present allowed, and of course the situation along the front line would dictate that such conferences would take place in a completely different time period.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And now that we've clarified your answers at 32815 of your testimony, I'd like to move on to a slightly different area but still keeping this operation from December 1993 in mind. In your testimony at 32576, you said your corps' objective was to defend their area of responsibility, and you said that a couple of times. Now, looking at this order which refers to ensuring the most favourable position for dividing the town of Sarajevo, would you agree with me if I was to suggest to you it's fair to say that defence of your area of responsibility wasn't your sole objective? Your objective was to maintain and consolidate and improve positions under control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I firmly know in terms of what was the mission of the corps and the task of the corps and what the corps could and wanted to carry out in terms of combat activities is what I already told you, and that is engagement was throughout the area at all points, was focusing on maintaining the territory that was under the control of the Romanija Sarajevo Corps. I know what you're after, because there's mention of division of Sarajevo here. Well, I can tell you simply when it comes to the division of Sarajevo, irrespective of whether anybody wanted or planned for that to happen, and I know that there was not -- there were no plans for that, division of Sarajevo is rubbish, is bunkum. Such activity could not be done and there was no need for it to be done. And it would not be reasonable to plan for such an activity, because it would entail huge losses and casualties on both sides, and I refute such claims that we were trying to enter Sarajevo to that extent that this is nothing to be discussed, because we neither wanted nor could nor planned to do so. We thought it would be -- made no sense and would entail huge sacrifices and casualties, and this is why we did not want to go into it. I -- I don't know what a kind of division is being referred to. You may ask Mr. Karadzic about that. A division does not have to mean territorial. There are other divisions of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So despite what looks like the plain wording of this order to SRK forces to set facts in place on the ground that would ensure a divided Sarajevo as part of a negotiated settlement in Geneva, you're now saying that division of the city was not one of the objectives?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is all I can say, and nobody ever issued an order to me in order to carry out certain combat actions for the purpose of dividing Sarajevo. I did not receive anything to that effect from anyone regardless of the level from which this could have come from. It could have just come from the commander of the Main Staff. And so I really couldn't tell you anything other than I remain by what I have said. And may I add, even had anybody ordered anything like that, I would have had to find a way not to accept that and to find another way of opposing that. It just wasn't realistic. The forces that we had available could not have made that happen, and we couldn't have embarked upon any kind of adventure in that sense, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're saying that even though the division of Sarajevo into Serb and Muslim parts was actually identified as one of the strategic objectives of the war by the Bosnian Serb leadership, that was not one of your corps objectives.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, I would like to ask you and the Trial Chamber to accept one of my sentences, a few words where I want to say the following: I am here in The Hague in the Detention Unit, and looking at my indictment when I was preparing for my trial, among other things I could see that there was some strategic goals being mentioned and so on and so forth. Just by chance I happened to find myself in the area where Mr. Krajisnik was as well, so I went. Well, if you can just try to follow me, what I want to try to tell you is something that can come out from my mouth only. I don't have any other information or assertions. I said, "Well, let me please see what these strategic goals are." And he took that down from the computer. He showed it to me. And I am telling this Trial Chamber that that was the first time that I specifically heard of those strategic goals, which means that during the events, the combat, throughout the whole period, no one issued anything to me or to General Galic. Nobody said, "Here are the goals. Go ahead, implement that." This was not the case with me or anyone else. We always had a way, a means of securing and protecting the existing area regardless of what the goals exist -- were, if any existed at all, but nobody imposed in practice for us to implement those goals through actions in the field, through combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll just wait a second until the general's had a chance to have a drink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you concentrate on answering the question. The question was this time whether it was one of the strategic objectives of the war by the Bosnian Serb leadership to divide Sarajevo into Serb and Muslim parts. So --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I -- may I ask to see where it is stated that these were strategic goals of the war, military strategic goals? If the question is varied to imply something that is not implied, then it places the witness into a difficult position. Had this been a military goal, the military would have known it. This was a political and strategic goal. Could we please see where it is stated that it was a military strategic goal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, could you put your question again, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The question was whether the general is now saying that the division of Sarajevo, ensuring, ensuring -- and I'll go back to my -- I'll go back to my notes and I'll characterize it the way I had initially. General, I'd like to put to you in the context of this document we've been looking at and SRK operations over the course of the war that your corps objective was as follows: To maintain and improve positions under your corps' control which would set facts in place on the ground to ensure the achievement of a divided Sarajevo as part of a negotiated settlement in Geneva or wherever the negotiations were taking place. So, General, it was your corps' job, wasn't it, to maintain the area, the existing area, to improve positions of your corps from that existing area which would set facts in place on the ground that would ensure the division of Sarajevo at the international negotiating table; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now it's all clear. I don't have any problem now to answer this question. The basic thing is to maintain the existing situation and to improve it. As for what would happen at the negotiations, what would be achieved there, that was up to somebody else, not up to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. In that sense, I can just give the answer that I completely agree with the point that the task was to maintain and improve the position which then makes it possible to, in negotiations, come to something that suits both sides, and for one side to fight for a particular status. So I would kindly ask you not to seek this as a military task to go into some sort of division. If the point is to say that the division was supposed to be achieved by military means, this is a task that was not issued by anyone nor was it possible to carry it out or to achieve by combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you were able to carry out your task because the existing area, your existing area, already effectively represented a division of the city, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "division" is something that I'm going to leave out of my answer. I'm talking about the area that is already. In my notes I wrote this already, that at the point in time when I came to the position of commander, all the issues were already, I would say, crystallised. There was a balanced ratio of forces, the conflict, and everybody knew what they wanted more or less and how they should manage their own forces. In this case, this picture of events or some sort of indicators of the territory, which in the initial period and during the first months of the war in 1992 and 1993 remained the same until the end, so there was no longer any question of division but it was more of a question of the sides staying wherever they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just in regard to your reference to meeting you and Mr. Sladoje, Cedo Sladoje, attended with Dr. Karadzic, and this is jumping forward in time to August of 1995, you said that -- at 32887 to 32889 of the transcript, you talked about how you didn't attend the colloquium of generals in Banja Luka because you were in combat, and when you returned to your command, your associates briefed you on what had happened, and you and Colonel Sladoje went to Pale where you went to see Dr. Karadzic. So could you just confirm in regard to that a couple of things that I think you may have left out. You actually didn't attend the colloquium because Dr. Karadzic told you not to go. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, that is not correct. Secondly, nobody could tell me to attend or not to attend, because they were not in a position to convey information to me that there would be a need to go and see Mladic. So I don't know if I understood you correctly, but I understood correctly that, if I may repeat that, that Mr. Karadzic told me -- I'm sorry, can you help me? What did you say that Mr. Karadzic told me, not to do what? Can you just, please, just tell me again?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That he prohibited you from attending the colloquium in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not forbid me. He didn't have the opportunity to do that. I don't know whether this is something that he thought about in his head, but the actual prohibition did not reach me, and even if it did reach me, I mean, it's a question of whether anybody can tell me whether to attend or not or to tell me how to conduct myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's correct, isn't it, that you and Colonel Sladoje didn't go to Pale on your own initiative. You went because you had been directed to go there with him by Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not receive any such order. I explained that when I came from mount Visojevica which is an area close to the most sensitive point, which was the Nisici plain, this is where I had an overview of the situation. I came quite late in the evening, I would say. Actually, quite late in the afternoon, around 18- or 1900 hours, and that is when Colonel Sladoje, Colonel -- the security chief came and explained what had happened during the day, that a meeting was scheduled with Mladic and that they were not able to tell me to prepare for the meeting and to go. Nothing else happened or was happening, and there was no other atmosphere being created other than us at that meeting attended by Lugonja and Cedo Sladoje reaching an agreement that the two of us should go to see Mladic, not because anybody ordered it. We just decided that on our own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at P2683. And just for the transcript, at page 25, line 16, it's Nisici with an N, as in November, as opposed with an M. So this document that we now see in front of us signed by Dr. Karadzic, General, is -- looks like it was a telegram dated 5 August, 1995, which was received in the corps at 5.00 p.m., directing you personally, together with your Chief of Staff who -- and Chief of Operations who was Colonel Sladoje, to come to the meeting in Pale in the president's office at 9.00. Now, you just said that nobody ordered you to go there. It seems that that's not the case, looking at this document; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that might seem like it to you, and here it looks as if this is something that's being confirmed. However, Sladoje and Lugonja did not show this document to me. Therefore, I did not know about the document, but I knew in this form that Mr. Karadzic -- well, this is how I understood it more or less, and it remains for me just to tell you that. Simultaneously -- and I don't see that from this document, by the way. So simultaneously as Mladic launched the initiative and summoned the generals to him, I understood from Cedo Sladoje, Colonel Cedo Sladoje, and Lugonja, that the same action, the same request was sent to the generals by President Karadzic, but I did not see this request in this way for me and the Chief of Staff individually. Let me just take a look. Evidently it states here what it states, but we didn't go pursuant to this, what is written here, because nobody showed me this. We agreed to go, to contact Mr. President in relation to that problem if anything can be amortised and a better solution found. So I stand by -- I mean, I'm not denying that this is something that is written down on the paper. This is a paper I did not have in my hand, so in agreement with the officers that I referred to in my office, there was no mention of going because the president was requesting it but it was our own decision. But they probably knew that this existed, so then we just set off by inertia, but I'm not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript, if it's important, on line 9, page 26, it says president's office, and here actually it says the cabinet of the president of the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's -- that's correct. If we could go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I find it very difficult to follow you. The president sent you -- the command sent to the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps urgently to come to a meeting, and how can -- how could a Chief of Staff or other staff not show this document to their commander? Could you assist me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's difficult for me to help you. I understand what you're saying, because that arrival of mine returned to the office implied a whole situation which in its way was serious, and the question of whether I should get this document or not or should be informed about it was not initiated. They informed me overall what was going on that day and that General Mladic was summoning people to him and General -- and Mr. Karadzic was summoning people to see him. So they did not show that in the form that this referred exclusively to me, but it was understood that President Karadzic was summoning people in his own way, in his own sense, to have a contact. I understood from them absolutely then, and that's why I didn't actually open up that question, that General -- that President Karadzic was summoning all the generals, but from here you can see that as far as the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps is concerned, in that case the invitation referred only to me. So I don't see. But they did inform me that it was a question of parallel invitations. One was making -- calling people to him and the other one was doing that as well. So of course it's understood that it cannot be quite clear. There was no question of to go or not to go. This all took place at a late point in time, and so perhaps because it was so late, perhaps it was superfluous for them to point out to me that this referred only to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just before the break, I'd like to move to another area, and it's about your service -- it refers to your military career, and it's about your service as operations officer with the Drina Corps in the spring of 1993. You mentioned that in your testimony in chief. Now, as the operations officer, you would have been familiar with Operation Udar which took place from February 14th to April 25th that year in the Drina valley; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A correction. I was not the duty operations officer at the corps. I was the chief of the operations sector in the corps. So I wasn't the duty operations officer. But, okay, this is not important. If by this name -- I cannot remember now -- well, I was informed about it. While I was there, I knew what was going on. I know that this code word Udar, you would need to remind me what this Udar referred to. Then I could tell you how much I knew, but I would like to underline that while I was at the corps, I didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, would you agree --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, in the transcript it says "I didn't know what was going on," but the witness said that "while I was in the corps, I knew what was going on." Line 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Udar was an operation to fortify the central Podrinje area, and it included operations against Cerska, Konjevic Polje, Sasa mine, and Srebrenica. You remember that now, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the outcome of the operation was that it was quite successful, and by mid-March, Drina Corps forces had routed the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina from all those areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let me just give an answer that would explain the whole thing. The area that we are discussing now or that I will be discussing is connected to a circumstance where the Army of Republika Srpska had a section of the road from Vlasenica towards Zvornik in this case that was cut off. This was in the area of Konjevic Polje, Pobudje, and towards Srebrenica, and to the north in the sector of Cerska. That area was held by the forces of the Bosnia and Herzegovina army, their 2nd Corps. I think it was the 83rd Division from Srebrenica, actually, and it was necessary to embark on active combat in order to open up a direct route from Vlasenica and, after all, from the inner areas of Republika Srpska. So because the road was cut off and the forces were separated in that area around that Konjevic Polje, then you would have some enclaves possibly created just like the Srebrenica enclave was created. So what happened was that a plan was drafted to carry out an operation from Sehovici, from the north, towards the south, and in that way to open up a route through Konjevic Polje so that we could have normal communication, a normal road towards Zvornik. Of course, the operation took a while. Mostly it was in early 1993, from March until I'm not sure when. Perhaps it was over by the end of April. I cannot be certain, but it's around that period. So the -- we managed to shift their forces and to open up the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours you, I see the time. I wonder if you'd like to take the break at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will. We will have a break for half an hour and resume at 3 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Before I continue with the general, I just want to respond to the intervention by Dr. Karadzic, Your Honours, where at page 22 he asked to see where it is stated that with respect to the strategic objectives that these were the strategic goals of the war, military strategic goals, and he asked where -- to see where it is stated that it was a military strategic goal, and in that regard I want to refer Dr. Karadzic to two exhibits that he tendered, Defence exhibits, the first being the analysis of combat readiness of the VRS in 1992, which is D325. Because I looked for this over the break, I wasn't able to identify the corresponding B/C/S pages, but Dr. Karadzic can find this information at e-court page 159 in English, the first full paragraph, where it says: "The strategic objectives of our war which were promptly defined and set before the Main Staff of the army of the RS, the commands and the units, served as a general guideline upon which we planned the actual operations and concerted battles." And Dr. Karadzic can additionally look to another one of his Defence exhibits, D825, which is a copy of a book by VRS Chief of Staff General Milovanovic called "My View of the War in Bosnia and Herzegovina," and at page 13 of the English and 13, in fact, of the B/C/S, refers to this six strategic objectives of the Serbian people as military objectives. So that's just to answer Dr. -- or to respond to Dr. Karadzic's intervention before we move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I took his statement to be asking that -- whether we can see the word strategic goal or military goal in that document, i.e., P4925, directive number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't, hence my response to that intervention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain what I meant. The original document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can take it up in your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it's not a matter for the witness. It was by way of reply to Mr. -- Ms. Edgerton's response. I asked about the original document of the 12th of May, 1992. Where in that document is it stated that these are wartime goals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, to go back to operation Udar, which we were discussing before we had the break, you indicated at page 30 that then you would have some enclaves possibly created as a consequence of the operation just like the Srebrenica enclave was created. And in fact as a consequence of the operation, that was exactly the case, wasn't it? The enclave of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde were created completely separated from each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer -- yes. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Inasmuch as this doesn't arise from anything in the direct examination, I'm wondering if this is for the purpose of credibility or whether this is being offered under Rule 90(H).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is a matter that goes to the witness's credibility, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And frankly, we could even -- General, you don't even need to answer that question at this moment. I'll move on still in relation to this operation. General, this Chamber has heard evidence in this trial about what happened in Cerska and Konjevic Polje during the course of this operation, and I'm going to put something additional to you and ask you a question following that, and what I'm going to put to you comes from 65 ter number 01219, the periodic report on the situation of human rights in the territory of the former Yugoslavia submitted by the Special Rapporteur of the commission on human rights, and the paragraph I'm going to put to you is at page 18 of the English, paragraph 87, and B/C/S page 19, but I'll read the paragraph to you. It says with respect to this operation: "Massive and repeated violations of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 were perpetrated in recent combat in Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina. These were carried out by Serb forces in Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica, in attacking and ambushing civilians attempting to flee their encirclement, in attacking the villages themselves, in refusing to allow humanitarian aid to enter, in refusing to allow the evacuation of the wounded, in attempting to link the above issues to the independent question of freedom of movement for Serbs in Tuzla." Now, General, you were one of the command team responsible for directing this operation that Mr. Mazowiecki reported on, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms and in an attempt to be crystal clear regarding this issue, I will not comment paragraph 87 and its wording. I'll come back to it at a later point. I joined the Drina Corps on the 4th of February, 1993. I remember that date since as today as well it is my birthday. That is why I remember my entry in the corps and engagement there. It happened then. You won't hold it against me if I say that as old acquaintances, I expected you to congratulate my birthday to me. I mentioned that because this operation, as you call Udar, and indeed that was its name, it had been planned, and the concept had been created for its implementation. I did not take part in the planning process though. As someone from the corps command, I observed the combat taking place according to the plan created by someone else at an earlier point, the people in question being the corps commander and his Chief of Staff at the time. The units were commanded by their respective commanders, as is understood, and it was implemented that way. I do know that there was a range of activities undertaken by the Muslim leadership in Bosnia-Herzegovina to portray Cerska as an endangered town, extremely endangered as part of that combat, trying to show that it was standard practice to attack towns in that way. I also know that General Morillon wanted to see for himself, to find out what that town was and what were those impermissible activities known to the public. He went to the area of Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, with respect, you actually don't seem to have come even close to answering my question, which was whether you could confirm that you were one of the command team responsible for directing this operation.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that, yes. I followed the activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on now to another area, and it's with respect to Sarajevo. Now, throughout your testimony, you repeatedly expressly denied that your forces targeted civilians in Bosnian government held Sarajevo. And that is referred to at transcript pages 32582, 32794, and 32833. Is it your evidence, General -- actually, let me ask you this: During the course of your service within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, so that would be from 1992 through to 1995, is it the case that neither Dr. Karadzic or General Mladic ever mentioned to you any of the concerns expressed by the international community to them over the targeting of civilians by shelling or sniping?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that's not what I'm going to say, that no one warned me of measures undertaken and that such activities be not permitted, that is to say that civilians become targets. I confirm that in entirety. They warned and asked for, et cetera. Of course, it was put to them by someone else as if things like that were happening. They in turn wanted to issue warnings and to prohibit such activity, that it should not be allowed. This fits completely with my assertion, which is that such activities were not undertaken by the factors in command of the SRK or by those who monitored and had any influence over the events in the area, in this case Mr. Mladic and Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Then I'd like to tell you about an incident in Sarajevo that took place on the 11th of July, 1995 [sic], and that was just five days after you took up office as Chief of Staff, and on that day Munira Zametica, a civilian, was shot twice from a firing position in the tower -- from the tower of the Serbian Orthodox Church in Velvina [phoen] while she was trying to get water from the Dobrinja River to do her washing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the sources of that are D673 and transcript page 29041 for the following, and the Chamber's heard evidence that that church was in the area of responsibility of your corps, general, and this woman's daughter, the victim's daughter came to testify before another Chamber of this Tribunal, and she told the Chamber in the Galic case that when she died, her mother was 47 years old, and on that day she was wearing a brown skirt, and when she came to find her mother still lying in the riverbed, her mother couldn't be helped or pulled to a safe area, and that was because bullets were continually hitting the water around here fired from the direction of the church. All right? So this was a victim, a civilian engaged in a civilian activity, shot not once but twice, and whose attacker continued to fire in the water around her to ensure -- which had the effect of ensuring she couldn't be saved. Now, would you agree with me, general, that this evidence shows the victim was deliberately targeted?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please remind me, was this on the 11th of July, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me, 1994, yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I noted down 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the transcript should read -- but you said 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Before you answer, yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe the date is July 11, 1993, according to scheduled incident number F(3).

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I completely misspoke. Correct. Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You understood well, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember my question? My question was whether you would agree that this evidence shows the victim was deliberately targeted.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, no victim, irrespective of the circumstances of his or her killing, if that person was civilian is something I cannot deny. As regards that term or that relationship, it is something I can't reconcile with my presence here. I can't possibly say that it is untrue. I won't even go into that. However, I will discuss the piece of information that simply enough someone simply took the Velvina church, which is in an valley, and it has an area where the church bells are, providing some kind of opportunity, and then one can always say, yes, there is engagement from the church. I have information that there was no activity from the church. It doesn't mean that I exclude the possibility of -- of late Munira being fired at. In the case of her death, there is nothing that I can assert other than say it couldn't have been done from the church. It was not allowed. I am positive on this. It's a definitive piece of information that I know. Nobody allowed any soldier to climb up the tower.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, my question was whether on the evidence that I read to you that the been put before the Galic Chamber as well as this Trial Chamber, you would agree that Ms. Zametica had been deliberately targeted. And I'll just review it again. She was a civilian. She was wearing a brown skirt. She was in a riverbed pulling water from the river. She wasn't shot once. She was shot twice, and she couldn't be rescued because her attacker continued to fire in the water around her. Does that sound like deliberate targeting to you, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A confirmation whether that was done deliberately or under other circumstances is something I cannot say or give. I exclude the possibility that things developed that way. Even if they had, it did not come about as a result of anyone's decision or anyone's issuing of tasks to a marksman to engage civilians. If under God knows what circumstances it was done by a soldier, he couldn't have been so instructed by his superior or permitted to do so. That is what I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, you continue to actually not answer my question other than say a confirmation whether this was done deliberately under other circumstances is something I cannot say or give, and yet you're able to -- you offer evidence or information that I would submit is purely speculative as to what might have gone on with respect to orders or soldiers' involvement. My question was simply related to the facts of what happened to this woman who was shot multiple times. If that wasn't direct targeting in the circumstances I've just given to you, what is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I wish you didn't assert that I was trying to be speculative or manipulative. That is not my task here. I do not accept that kind of assertion before the Court. That is why I kindly ask you to refrain from doing so. That was one thing. Another thing, you cannot ask me to confirm -- well, I confirm that any engagement of civilians is impermissible and that as such cannot be justified. I can confirm, though, what our policy and practice was --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, let me stop you there --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- all rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- because you've said you've given evidence about what your policy and practice was over and over again, and we'll move on to another incident that happened the very next day, so 12 July 1993. And it happened at a well in Dobrinja where the Zametica family actually would most frequently get their drinking water, and that's T 3487 of the victim's daughter's evidence in the Galic case. Now, on 12 July, 13 people were killed and 14 wounded when an 82-millimetre mortar shell was fired at a hundred civilians who were waiting in line to get access to this well to get their water, and an individual, a civilian, Rasim Mahonjic and his wife and two daughters were waiting in line for water at this well when it happened, and in his testimony at the Galic case in transcript page 7329 to 7240, he talked about what happened. His evidence was that his two daughters went to join the line at 2.00 a.m. so that they could get to the pump on time, and he and his wife followed at 10.00 that morning, and they waited together in line throughout the day until about 4.00 p.m., and Mr. Mahonjic and his family were second in line to get to the pump. There was only one family ahead of them when the shell fell, and it killed his wife and his daughters among the other victims. Now, General, people were waiting in line, in the water line in this case, for as much as 14 hours to get to the pump. Now, based on the evidence I've given you, would you agree with me that that's an example of direct targeting of a group of civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, you're basically trying to extract answers from me about something I am unaware of. I simply don't know. The indicators that I would require would have to be much more specific and detailed save for the fact that people waited for hours on end to get water. I do not exclude that intention that everything had to do with water, firewood, and burials, but it's a different matter to say that somebody awaited someone else at a certain place in order to do something that would go against acceptable conduct vis-a-vis civilians. Whatever happened had to have been investigated in order to find out what happened and who was to blame. That kind of procedure was within General Galic's remit. Now, to what extent and how well he did so is something I don't know. The way you presented this, there's nothing else for me to tell you other than to repeat that it was unacceptable --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, General --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and that there's no other way for me to view it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I won't ask you to repeat yourself again, but I thought, General, as a career officer who's been recognised for your service in the battle-field, you would have been able to assess the evidence that I'd given you about these two incidents as to whether or not they sounded like examples of direct targeting. Is that the case or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm going to object to this question because that's really unfair to a witness. Civilians are standing in a line and there's a shelling. Unless you know whether it was deliberate, whether there was an accident, which side it came from, whether there were multiple rounds that were adjusted to attack the civilians, you can't answer that question. So I don't think there's any probative value to the question ask that you exclude it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd actually like to move on, Your Honours, if I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, a correction in the transcript. In line 23, page 40, the witness said [in English] "that it was unacceptable if it happened." "If it happened," this did not find its way in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, in your testimony in chief, you also repeatedly denied that Sarajevo-Romanija Corps forces shelled civilian areas, and by way of reference that's at transcript pages 32582, 83, and 32752. And in your testimony you referred not only to areas but also used the words sectors and neighbourhoods, but just with respect to that first word, "areas," and when you mean to describe a civilian area, how broad is an area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, will you agree with me when I say that I finally and officially -- officially treat Sarajevo in its entirety, the whole town, this whole area, all settlements, as a civilian area? I am trying to express myself in an original way by saying that the term "area" and "zone," et cetera, whether it's civilian or not, this is something I reject. For me this whole of Sarajevo is a civilian area. Why? Because in that town and throughout that area, civilians resided there. That's one thing. Another thing, if we make -- may make a distinction between military targets and everything else, a military target is a place where fire is opened from and where groups and forces engage in combat from a certain area. This is something we can discuss, whether there were targets and could be a target at a certain point in time. In this case, I'm not dealing with the term "area." I'm not treating it as such whether -- irrespective of whether it's 100 metres, 1.000 metres, if it's a certain locality or not. If there is a civilian there, it is deemed a civilian area. But if fire is opened from that area, then an assessment will have to be made what to do with that target which then constituted a military target. There would be a solution. There would be a procedure put in place not to put civilians in danger when it's possible. If it's not, then an absolute assessment will have to be made if there would be collateral damage which would outweigh a military mission to be accomplished, then this is abandoned. A parallel is drawn between military advantage and success and the goal -- or target which appears or if there is a situation which may lead to civilians being exposed to an impermissible action if that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you said at transcript page 32582: "We were not allowed to shell a civilian area nor indeed would we have chosen to shell a civilian area. The SRK didn't do that. Wherever there were civilians, that was not a target for us. We never fired at those areas," your evidence is now that you meant to refer to the city of Sarajevo as a whole; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reiterate in the final analysis, wherever there are civilians, that area is a civilian area, and since there were civilians throughout Sarajevo, then my response coincides with this. But please, through -- I've been through this procedure. My attorney-at-law, my legal counsel, tried to put forward an argument that the -- that Sarajevo was a military area. I tried to disabuse him of that notion. I realised that the Trial Chamber kept on asking him about that and that he could put forward no quality answers to that. Well, even in my utterances you can find "area" and zone, but this is a legacy of my background. Now I am giving you an official explanation and distinction between area, zone, military target, and civilian area. I'm sure that this is perfectly clear to everybody listening.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were there any no-fire zones in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were. There were zones, several of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Tell us what those were.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about zones but areas, space, parts of the town. There were no incidents where fire was opened at civilians. For instance, in Urijan Bedina Street there were no such incidents. On Bjeliva [phoen], in Jarcedol, in Bostarici. Parts of Mejtas. Not Mejtas in its entirety but parts of it. There were no combat activities or firing being opened at -- be it on military structures or civilians. Well, I know that area, but I cannot name it, the name escapes me. Well, it was Vasin Han. I'm not sure whether I listed all of them. I've not, but those were the areas where there were no incidents of shells falling there or rounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So let's talk about these military targets you referred to, because you talked about them in different ways in your testimony in chief. First of all, you talked about command posts. At T2 -- transcript page 32553, you said: "The number of command posts within Bosnian-held Sarajevo was 275." So my question to you is: Is it your evidence that that's the case throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that at those times, from 1992 to 1995, you observed and identified all 275?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely that is no longer an assertion whether we located each and every of them. We just received intelligence about their location. We knew at that there were certain command posts that were not visible.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is it -- is it your evidence that you shelled them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Providing you information about the existence of such a military command structure that was effective in that area at the time is something else. Those were military targets, and they could not -- could be targeted, but it's another matter, and it's not been confirmed, which those -- which targets of those command posts were targeted and which were not. If there was no danger emanating from those areas even if such targets were legitimate, then we had no need to act against those localities.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've just said, as I understood you, that with respect to these 275, that was on the basis of intelligence you received about their location and not necessarily on the basis of observation; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a combined effort. It's a combined process of getting information. That information was obtained through intelligence or through observation, and then you put together the pieces of that jigsaw puzzle. Many localities, many points, were highly visible. There would be frequent goings-on. For instance, 12 brigades, command post, it's Dobrovoljacka Street. You could see it and you could see the frequency of the comings in and goings out of the commanders, where shifts were organised, security detail being replaced, companies and special --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But it --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- forces being sent from there --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It stands to reason - and not accepting for a moment your number of 275 is correct - you're not saying that these command posts were of equal sophistication by any stretch, are you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is irrelevant how sophisticated in terms of equipment they were because a company commander's command post could not be as equipped as a command post of a corps or brigade commander. Of course, there are differences in terms of manpower, in terms of security detail and equipment, and in terms of presence of the commander at that particular command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you refer to these command posts, whether or not you had observations, I take it you're generally referring to buildings, some kind of structures, are you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't need to be. Certain command posts could be in shelters, in bunkers, in parts of facilities which allow them to work and provide certain level of security and safety. But first and foremost, they were located in economic facilities, schools --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now -- now, General, let's just try and focus on my question. You said you didn't shell all of them. How many did you shell of these structures?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You really cannot get that kind of information. Really, I don't know. I don't have the information about that. I cannot even confirm whether we shelled either. We did not shell them. But any target which constituted danger, it was targeted, but if it was considered to be a target in this form, then no action -- if there's no threat, no action would be put in place against it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you targeted those shelters, bunkers, or other facilities, you targeted them with mortars; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know quite well that you fire what you have at your disposal. I'm not confirming here, neither that we shelled them with mortar nor with cannon or any other device. I'm not specifying the type of arms we used. Let me go back to my assertion that command posts mainly were not targeted. No fire was opened at them. Why? Because, for instance, the command post at Sedrenik was located in a coffee house, very famous coffee house where certain circles gathered and spent days and nights there. That command post could have been targeted by any device available to us, but it never was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, could we go back to my question of what you targeted those command structures with. When you said you fire them with what you have at your disposal, do you mean to say --
