utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you mean to say you targeted them with whatever you had?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The witness stated that mainly they were not targeted. He did not say that they targeted them with everything at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will you ask the question again, or --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, those command posts that you targeted, do you mean to say, based on your answer that you fire with what you had at your disposal, that you targeted them with whatever you had?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we are getting anywhere. We're not making progress if we continue in the same vein. If you want me to say that this happened by using a mortar, then I have to be specific about justifying reasons to use a mortar. You cannot use direct fire if you fire a mortar. It has a certain curve that the shell follows. I did say that command posts were not targets. However, technically how this could have been done is what I tried to explain to you just now. If it's open area, it can be targeted with a device which can fire direct -- directly, not indirectly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Those that were targeted, what did you target them with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are -- you are discussing command posts, and I said that we did not use anything to target command posts.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in your testimony in chief, you went into a long analysis based on a couple of things to come to this figure of 275 command posts. So if you didn't target them, General, what was the point of the analysis?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of that analysis was for you as a person in your capacity to get a picture and to draw a conclusion that the type of charges and assertions against me that shelling was indiscriminate and merciless. My point was -- is that there were many possible [Realtime transcript read in error "impossible]" targets throughout area, and that my choice of determining the targets to be shelled was based on the fact that they were endangering or threatening our defensive positions and if that target constituted a threat and this was when it became a target.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't want to leave that figure of 275 yet, because it seems to me, General, and maybe you can confirm this, that it seems to me that you arrived at that figure of 275 purely on the basis of extrapolations from military doctrine. You conducted your own independent doctrinal analysis; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see a problem in asking the question on how this figure was determined in our analysis about the existence of that number of command posts. They confirmed themselves the existence of such command posts is implied, because there's no structure or unit at a certain level which would not have its own command. Nobody can function or use units without their command structure, and since they exposed their materiel and their personnel, it was easy to obtain information about the existence of such structure. And also, this analysis talks not about the type of targets but the stage of development of command structures and the way that units were being used and combat operations being carried out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, if I may, intervention about the transcript. Line 19, page 48, the witness did not say that there were "impossible targets throughout" but "incountless" or "innumerable" targets throughout the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, General, based on what I understand from what you just said, it seems that your analysis to the effect that each major unit would have three command posts is based to some extent on ABiH documents as well as your own thinking; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on my thinking but on the hard data. A division command must have separate --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Whose data? Whose data, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? I did not get this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You said that analysis is based on hard data. Where's the data?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The data that there is a 12th Division that exists. You cannot deny that. If that division exists, it must be structured in such a way so that it has its operational parts which conducts combat activities and logistics or the rear which performs logistics duties. And of course it has to have its area of operation, because it -- they cannot follow from the Dobrovoljacka Street well what is going on at Zuc if they're interested in what is going on, and this is why they have three command posts.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, I wonder where's the data, General? Where's the documents that you base this on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the data must be with you. I don't know which data you're asking me about it, because data that the 12th Division existed or the 5th, I'm taking this as an example. This is not something that should be re-examined. If you're questioning whether they existed or not, then that's the path that needs to be taken, how things turned out that way, who is dealing with the command and all of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, I'd actually like to examine that a little bit, and maybe we could have a look at D633. It's a document dated 25 October 1993, and it's an ABiH 1st Corps command order for defence. Now, if we can go over to page 3 of the English, paragraph 5.1, and B/C/S page 2 in the same paragraph, please. General, the end of paragraph 5.1 in this document you see in respect of this operation, you see that for the 1st Motorised Brigade, at the bottom of paragraph 5.1, only one command post. If we could scroll down in English so we see the bottom of paragraph 5.2. Look, General, only one command post for the 2nd Brigade in the Kras area. Could we go over to the next page, please. The 102nd Motorised Brigade has only one command post in the wire factory area. The 5th Motorised Brigade has only one command post in the Dobrinja area. So it seems, General, based on this document that not only are your mathematics off, but you relied on doctrine because it actually inflates the number of command posts; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that nothing of this is in dispute, because when issuing an assignment to his troops, subordinate troops, the corps commander is obliged to state where their basic command post is. The other command post locations is something that he does not have to specify, and he doesn't need to change the location. So it doesn't have to be in the place where the corps commander says it has to be, but it can stay at the place where the brigade commander located it already.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the second thing is this is nothing that has to do with strategy. Can you please allow me to finish. You interrupted me. So this is not being taken out of the context of the rules, the strategy of combat. It states here what it states in some of their other documents. Secondly, all of these units change their structure, as you are well aware, in the second half of 1994, whereas here you're talking with me and asking me about documents from 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My information --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- let me stop you right there. You specifically said, and I can find you the transcript reference if you like, you specifically said, I think during the first day of your testimony in chief, that the structure didn't change the areas of responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to be quite clear what we're talking about. I don't know what you're thinking. It's not true that it didn't change. If I said that, then I must have thought about something else. I don't know what. You need to remind me what I was thinking of. The Armija B and H restructuring as a whole occurred in the second half of 1994, as I said. That was when so-called Caco's brigade was disbanded as well as these other groups and hordes that had a different connotation, and then they tried to place them under military structure properly as things should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So then I've just shown you a document from 1993 that lists the brigades as having one command post, yet you said in your earlier answers to me that this figure of 275 was a figure that was constant throughout the war. This document is evidence to the contrary, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's contrary in your opinion, because something is missing. It was left out from here --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the sense of --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- when things are being specified.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's look at one of your own documents, P5968, and by "your own" I mean a Sarajevo-Romanija Corps document. It's an operations order by General Galic, and it's dated 26 January 1994. Now, if we could go over to page 2 in both languages, please. This lists SRK data, hard data, as to the number of command posts per brigade. Look, General, at the bottom of the page. The 1st Motorised Brigade is listed as having one command post. The 2nd doesn't even have one listed in this document. The 5th is also listed as having one command post. The 105th, one command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go over to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The 104th, again one command post. It seems if we're to accept your evidence that something was missing from the document generated by the ABiH, it seems as though General Galic is actually missing something in his operations order as well, or, General, is your math wrong?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what your conclusion will be or how you're trying to dispute the number of command posts. I stand by saying that it's quite certain that these units had a developed command structure and as such it had to exist and it had to function regardless of if it was written down in any paper or not. You cannot manage with one. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had its main command post in Lukavica and the rear command posts in -- post in Pale. This is a requirement that nobody can leave out, and you cannot merge these two structures that they would work together. They have to work separately, each in its own sphere. So I don't see anything of dispute here. I assume that what concerns you is this number of 275 command posts. If I had said that just 55 command posts there were for battalions, then does that not indicate something quite significant in terms of numbers? If we add company commander command posts, then the numbers progress.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, to progress --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I wouldn't --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To progress, let's look at D2792. It's a document from 11 June 1995, and you've seen it before. It's the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina 1st Corps command's attack order, and you've said a couple of times now -- you've referred a couple of times to the changing structure of the 1st Corps in 1995. So let's have a look at that. After the structure has changed and the corps has gone from brigade to division formation, if you will go over to page 4 of the English translation and page 3 of the B/C/S. There, starting at paragraph 5.1 you see the first mention of two command posts, a main in the Astra sector and a forward command post in Sokolje village. Paragraph 5.2, again two command posts per brigade. So, General, in fact it looks likes the documents from both the ABiH and the SRK show that the scenario you've suggested of every major formation having three command posts has never actually been the case as far as the ABiH 1st Corps is concerned.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite the contrary, it was always the case, especially as far as forward command posts are concerned. Therefore, those commands and the commanding officers cannot do anything or monitor anything from the centre of the city unless they have a forward group of people who would monitor and direct action from a forward command post. This is a rule that I think we will not really get far if you don't take that rule into account. As for the operational part of the command --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and the rear command --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- General --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- right at the beginning, this is something that is separate.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You asked -- you indicated -- when I asked you for the hard data, you indicated that we probably had it, and I've now shown you the hard data about the number of command posts for the different military formations within Sarajevo, and the hard data shows that even up until 1995, the major formations never had more than two command posts. So you're contradicted by the hard data, aren't you, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that, but ultimately I can say that even that is no longer an issue, whether they had three or two. Don't forget, Ms. Edgerton, that they had to have had more locations and axes, because I as corps commander had to have one forward command post at Nisici, one forward command post at Trnovo, and one main basic command post in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The need --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll move on, because -- without spending any more time on the numbers, recalling what you said, your assertion earlier that you didn't target most of these in any case. But still on the subject of targeting, you talked about -- at 32581, you talked about ABiH forces using civilian facilities including the Kosevo Hospital, schools, nurseries, commercial buildings, shops, and private homes for military purposes, and at 32700, referred to essentially the same thing. So my question about that is did you fire at those facilities? And let's go through one by one. Did you fire at the Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you fire at schools?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you fire at nurseries?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Commercial buildings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So hearing that, I want to ask you then would you agree that the reason you didn't fire at those facilities is because of the risk to civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Choice of targets is a completely different action. When you choose a target, then you establish everything, and I think I mentioned this several times already, you mention the degree of threat, the level of fire from it, the area around it, how many civilian -- of the civilian population are there around it, how much of a threat the target is to our positions. I think that you understand that very well. All the things that we had to note in order to make an assessment whether one was permitted to fire at the target or not. And mostly this indicates that these schools from where somebody was in command, we didn't fire at them, but if there was a school where on the roof of the school there was a device with sandbags, meaning that there was fire over the heads of one's own units, then that fire was that much of a threat that we had to neutralise it by our own fire. You asked here about command posts. They were mostly not fired at, but perhaps we can differentiate a little bit from -- between general targets, fire targets, and command posts. Then no, no, no, no, means no at a school if officers are having a meeting there. But if there is coming -- fire coming from there, that is a completely different circumstance and it's a different type of target. It's not the same kind of fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I asked you whether or not you fired -- I specifically asked you whether or not you fired at schools and you said no, but your answer now is yes. So my question is: How would you respond to mortars being fired from a school?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you cannot fire from a school. A mortar cannot be fired from a building. It's a question -- doesn't take it wrongly, but it's not a professionally put question. You cannot place a mortar in a school and fire it from a school. It can be near a school, behind a school, and so on and so forth. And then the situation is different in terms of that mortar than when we're talking about a building.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How would you respond to mortars being fired within, as you said in your testimony in chief, 100 metres from a school?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would like to suggest that we cannot really proceed this way, but this is your methodology, and I respect that. If I said 100 metres, I am trying now to ask you to forget those 100 metres. It's possible that I wasn't precise enough. However, it all comes down to, I repeat, and I don't know if it's rational to keep repeating that one studies a target to see what sort of a danger it poses and what is around it. The main factor in adopting a position is that there are no civilians near the target which could be the object of fire when one fires at the target. So this is something that is avoided unless we're talking about -- well, it all comes down to one mortar here. That one mortar was never the issue, but it was a mortar battery numbering four to six weapons when you would get quite heavy fire from there. And then one would evaluate such targets and see when and how one would fire at such target. But even in such a case, it was absolutely a thing to avoid having civilian casualties by firing in the vicinity of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So is your answer that you would -- you would respond to mortars being fired from within 100 metres of a school with mortars?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where you get that I would respond by mortar fire or that I said that the choice of weaponry would be a matter of what weaponry was available at the given moment. I did not say that we would respond to mortar fire with mortar fire from our side. It's something that I didn't say nor can this be exercised in the field nor should it be done in this way. It doesn't have to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you excluding by your answer that you responded to mortar fire with mortars?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not ruling that out. It just means that you shouldn't hold me to these 100 metres. I understand what you're trying to say by using the 100 metres and then if you miss then you hit a different target. This is not what I'm talking about. I'm talking about the type of fire that we would respond to their fire. This is up to the commander who is endangered and up to the weapons that he had at that time. I mean, we didn't have enough weaponry to be able to choose we're going to use that or something else. They can be also hit by anti-aircraft weaponry operating from the ground if there was a firing line and a situation where he could silence that mortar. But these things are not necessarily connected.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you don't want us to hold you to the 100 metres, let me ask you this: How near a civilian or a civilian object would you fire?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope that you're not expecting an answer. I don't have a different answer. Choice of target cannot be such that the civilian structure suffers from our fire. That decision cannot be made. I'm not ruling out at all the possibility of it happening for different reasons, but in making the decision and issuing the task to open fire, that action could not happen by saying, well, let's hope it won't happen and taking a certain risk. One would aim to hit a target as a result of which the population would not suffer. Innocent civilians would not suffer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just looking at the time. I'm wondering if -- this is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 17 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, when we left off before the break, we left off before the break with you giving evidence of your efforts to avoid civilian casualties in Bosnian-held Sarajevo and the scrupulous proportionality assessments you made in that regard when it came to shelling. And you said that the choice of target cannot be such that the civilian structure suffers from our fire. And, General, with respect, the weight of evidence the Chambers of this Tribunal have heard is completely to the contrary, and I'm going to put some of that to your recollection and I'm going to ask you a question. They have heard with respect to Bosnian-held Sarajevo that the whole city was peppered with damage from shelling or gunfire. Almost no building had windows, many of the larger buildings had holes in them, and they were splashed from shrapnel from mortar rounds. Areas of the city that had not been militarily contested were often scattered with pockmarks from shelling or gunfire. They have received evidence that throughout the war, forces, SRK forces, made no distinction --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me, and the source for the first quote is P820, paragraph 27.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: They've received evidence that throughout the war SRK forces made no distinction between military and civilian targets. Anything that moved, including civilian pedestrians, came under fire. Hospitals, schools, and historical buildings received direct artillery, tank and mortar fire on a regular basis, while houses, apartments, and gathering places such as markets and waterlines would be shelled without seeming pattern. Nobody knew when and where a shell would hit, so every place was dangerous. And that's transcript page 8170 in this trial, General Brigadier General Fraser. They have heard, the Judges in this Tribunal have heard the testimony of individuals who saw random and indiscriminate spelling by your forces throughout Bosnian-held Sarajevo. One witness, a Dutch military officer, said: "It's the fact that I saw that we, my team, I myself and my people, we witnessed falling rounds, especially mortar rounds, throughout the city in a random pattern, not in a way that you combat military targets with." And further on he continues: "It is what I witnessed during those periods. I don't know why the Serb commanders did it. I don't know what orders they had, but the fact is what I saw is that they were random firing with single rounds or a few rounds on areas where there were no military targets whatsoever." And that's transcript page 9345 to 46 in this trial, the evidence of Lieutenant-Colonel Konings. And similarly, Major Pyers Tucker saw artillery under the control of your forces being used on one hand in support of attacks by your infantry but also saw it being used to fire all over the city at targets that had nothing to do with the actual attack. The impression he gained was that the purpose of this shelling was in order to intimidate the population of the city in general and the government in power and to break their will to resist, and that's P4203. Another witness described the most common form of shelling he experienced during his time in Sarajevo as shelling that was constant but a relatively low bombardment by your forces with no identifiable military purpose. It seemed intended to keep the civilian population of Sarajevo locked down, vulnerable, fearful, and isolated. It wasn't entirely random. Sometimes targeting certain neighbourhoods from one day to the next but otherwise there was --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wonder -- I wonder, your Excellencies, how one can answer a question as complex as this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber was discussing this. So shall we stop there and hear from the witness or will you put a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I ask a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. If the general is able to answer the question. Yes, what is your question, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, the weight of the evidence before this Tribunal as to the shelling by your forces and targeting of civilians in Sarajevo is massively contrary to the evidence you've given today, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. That's absolutely an impossible question. First of all, to spend two pages of transcript to ask a question is absolutely unacceptable and unheard-of, but then to finally ask a question about the weight of evidence in this trial. He has not been sitting through this trial. He has no way to answer that question. We've just wasted about 10 minutes, and I hope you'll consider that if they ask for additional time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: May I rephrase?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, this evidence shows that your forces were doing exactly what you said they weren't; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I don't think he can comment on evidence he hasn't heard in total. I don't think it's appropriate for him to be asked to comment on it. There's a more direct way to ask these questions. I think you should instruct the Prosecutor to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, to simply read out the transcript and turn it into effectively an enormous compound question, it's very difficult because you then asked a question at the end which in a sense demands a yes or no answer, Does it contradict that which I've said. It's putting the witness into an extremely difficult position. It might be better to formulate it something like this: General, bearing in mind the thrust of the evidence that's been read out to you, if the Chamber found it was accurate evidence, wouldn't that contradict your statement that there was no indiscriminate fire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was the question from the Prosecution. Could you answer the question then, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect to the people who testified, and the questions or assertions put forth by Ms. Edgerton, my answer would be that I was hoping for this situation to arise so that I can address the issue. Neither Ms. Edgerton nor the esteemed gentlemen who came to testify had an opportunity to view the entire situation in its full complexity and the way both sides had to assess it, on the one side the SRK and the other the 1st Corps of the army of BH. I think I will be sufficiently precise if I said that if things had taken place indeed the way it was portrayed here, that events unfolded without measure, Sarajevo would have been razed to the ground. The area itself could not sustain it if this were proven to be true. It was not. Such engagement did not come about. And it does not fall within the concept of what our position or policy was. What I know only is that we did not allow such activity, such behaviour. For the most part, without interpreting things in any other way as regards my period between 1992 and 1995 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When engaging targets, that is something I want to discuss here to confirm and whether we actually engaged in such conduct. There is nothing to hide. We didn't behave this way, and things did not develop this way. No atmosphere was created to the extent that people were being driven crazy there. One cannot put such assertions that our activity, our engagement went along those lines. Such a procedure, such conduct did not take place, and it cannot be accepted that every part of town was targeted like that every day and that the procedure was something that went on day after day. It was all portrayed in such a way as to show that we enacted a campaign of terror against the population while setting aside all the other aspects such as standing ground and opposing the other side, their 1st Corps. This kind of position, this kind of thesis cannot be sustained, and I am ready to address it from a number of viewpoints. However, if one wants to create an anathema as regards the military conduct of the SRK, such as that it was a bestial organisation, it's certainly not a good way to try and prove anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last line, actually line 3, should be "bestial," and just above that I believe he mentioned terrible, a terrible situation, a terrible atmosphere which did not make its way into the transcript I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, I'd like to show you a document you drafted. It's P2668. And, General, you've just said in answer to this question that it cannot be accepted that every part of town was targeted like that every day and procedure, the procedure we were discussing, was something that went on day after day. Now, this document was issued by you on the 19th of July, 1995, and it relates to the rational expenditure of ammunition. If you go to page -- paragraph 2 of this document, about halfway through the paragraph it says: "That is why we very often fire at inhabited settlements and specific buildings when there are no combat actions whatsoever spending vast quantities of ammunition without paying attention to the fact that we will not have anything to stop the enemy when it comes to mounting a decisive defence." And if you go over to the next page in both languages, I think paragraph 4 on page 2, this reads: "In order to achieve a surprise effect and inflict the highest enemy losses, produce strong, planned, concentrated fire from several weapons from different directions at a specific time instead of firing one or two weapons for an hour at the same target. So, General, this document represents -- is actually an acknowledgement that your forces were indeed targeting the city in the way you've just said they weren't.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that there is no map. It is my conclusion that you lost sight intentionally or unintentionally because, of course, it is your goal to lead me into providing a wrong answer. The SRK covered a specific area that these warnings referred to, and they also referred to such areas where there were no settlements or where there were very small abandoned settlements which housed only their forces, that is, when we are discussing some rural areas just outside Sarajevo. You are now putting all of this in the context of Sarajevo and its residential buildings, but it definitely doesn't mean that. If you would kindly return the first item on the screen. I think I was cautioning them not to do it unnecessarily. Well, whoever is receiving an order needs to be told clearly that they should not open fire unnecessarily, that it may be detrimental if one even ponders opening fire in the context that doesn't require it. That is why I said that there should be no pointless targeting of inhabited areas. One could only conclude the following, that we didn't need to and that we had to in order to achieve success, as my people would do it, as if we were just beating around the bush to act pointlessly. For such kind of activity, while we didn't have that much ammunition and we didn't act that way because, as it says here, that conditions needed to be created for a specific moment in time which may pose a much greater threat in terms of enemy breakthrough. So all of our instructions and all of our enforcing of regulation revolved around the concept of proper conduct in the right manner, in the right spirit. That's what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, this --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that that's what the document is trying to show and that it wasn't the witness who was trying to say it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The document was authored by the general. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, with respect, as much as the warning cautions your forces against spending vast quantities of ammunition as if they had it in abundance, if you look, if you go back over to page 1 in both languages, if you look at paragraph 2, it refers -- it specifically says: "That is why we very often fire at inhabited settlements and specific buildings when there are no combat actions whatsoever." On its face, General, the document doesn't lend itself to any other interpretation than inhabited settlements were being targeted when there was no combat action underway; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Incorrect. If I may, I'd like to present my approach to this. When issuing orders to my units, I have to warn them in such a way which would put them in the right situation, because they don't know whether it referred to their specific activity or the activity of a unit that is adjacent to it in terms of the SRK. And they should receive their own information or caution that if a specific person or a unit should try to engage targets in that way, that it simply cannot be done randomly or blindly, if I may put it that way. It may appear to be that way to you, but I do know that those units had to be cautioned and provided with instruction in different ways so as not to find themselves in a situation where they would behave like that and not to make it a practice. Actually, they always had to bear in mind that it was simply not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll just move on to another area, General, and it's an area you spent a lot of time dealing with in your examination-in-chief, and it's about air-bombs and the air-bomb shelling you ordered on 6 April 1995. Now, General, you clearly know something about these air-bombs, don't you, and how they operate, because as a commander ordering their use you would be required to be familiar with these assets. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: These air-bombs are really area assets, aren't they? Area weapons.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both from the air and from the ground, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: They're -- let me rephrase. These air-bombs, like -- not unlike mortars, are meant as area weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't have to be that way. If you're targeting a specific target which is stronger and profitable target with large number of people, we are not discussing area here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the air-bombs incident on Dositejeva Street, you said, and it was at transcript page 32780, that if it had indeed fallen there, it would have caused much greater destruction than it did. So maybe given that, you can tell us exactly with a kind of destructive power these bombs had.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an asset containing a large quantity of explosive, and its effect covers a larger area, and it produces more effects than mortars or other pieces of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what kind of quantity of explosive does it contain? How much?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two types of such bombs. 100 kilograms one and 250 kilogrammes the other. That quantity does not refer to the quantity of explosives but the total mass of the asset. I could not confirm here whether 250 kilogrammes or 100 kilogrammes would be 100 kilogrammes or 250 kilogrammes of explosive. These are technical specifications. What I know are the types of air-bombs. What I don't know is what precisely they contain.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. And you obviously know a little bit about their accuracy, because in your evidence in chief at transcript page 32773, when Dr. Karadzic asked you where the bombs were fired from, you said they were fired from your corps area of responsibility behind the lines of the units in the trenches, and if there were residential areas on the axis, these bombs would go across those areas, but those situations were mostly avoided and your forces chose localities where such aerial bombs would have to overfly only your units and those were circumstances, you said, that required caution, and it had to be made sure that there was a high degree of precision, otherwise the bomb may have landed on your forces. So clearly based on your evidence, you were aware of a certain measure of risk with regard to the launching and landing of that air-bomb, a risk to your forces and Serb-held areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you misunderstood that utterance. If it is said that one of the reasons why accuracy has to be achieved and high level of precision, it is that very reason. If there's no accuracy and precision, they could fall on our forces, on our territory. This is not in contravention, neither does it change the situation which shows that we were working on upgrading those air-bombs, introducing electronics and expertise of experts, calculating the tables so that they may be turned into a reliable assets when used.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't think there was any misunderstanding, General. You were clear in your evidence that situations where the bombs might fly across residential areas were mostly avoided. That's because the bomb might have landed on them, isn't?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Naturally I know what you're after.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, we also talked -- or you also discussed in your evidence in chief at 32776 and 32777 some of the other air-bombs incidents apart from the incident on 7 April 1995. In particular, you talked about the one on Majdanska Street on 24 May. At transcript page 32778, you said that the distance in this case, the Majdanska Street incident, 130 or 140 metres to the residential building was far enough to be safe. It couldn't be damaged by your action. People would be unhappy about it, but there were no casualties. So 130 to 140 metres is your acceptable safe radius for the use of these bombs. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me it is acceptable that whoever finds himself 100 or more metres, that that person would not be in danger. One hundred metres from the place of detonation. There's no doubt about that. But let's not lose sight of the fact that I was in the vicinity of detonation sites when NATO air-bombs fell, and I survived without a scratch. I know what those air-bombs effect was when they tried to destroy certain facilities, in this particular case military facilities. Without a direct hit, their effect is just to -- to dig a crater. I'm not trying to belittle the effect of those air-bombs, but these are not assets that would have unlimited destructive power. I ventured into those craters of eight NATO air-bombs at Hadzici and Jahorinski Potok and at bridges, et cetera, et cetera. For instance, they could not destroy those bridges using those air-bombs, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll get to your presence at Sarajevo around the time of the NATO bombing a little bit later, but I want to stay for the time being a little bit earlier in 1995 at the time of -- around the time of these incidents. I actually on the subject of the safe radius would like to show you a document. It's P1299, and it's dated 26 April, 1995. And it will be two quick documents in succession. So this is an extremely urgent piece of correspondence to you from General Mladic asking for an explanation, saying you're to inform him -- saying he's in possession of information that you are planning to use two air-bombs against enemy targets and settlements in the area of Sarajevo in the evening of 26 April, and directing you to inform him whether this information is correct, who ordered it, why, the planned use of the weapons, and the beginning of the operations in Sarajevo. Now, once you've had a chance to look through that document, I'd like to go to another one related to this. And do you see actually, General, on the top right-hand corner of the document handwritten there's a notation that Colonel Tadija gave a partial reply? That would be Colonel Tadija Manojlovic your chief of artillery, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just let us know when you've had a chance to look at this document, General, and we'll go on to the next one. And General, if you ever need to have this enlarged, all you need to do is say, because our colleagues here can enlarge the image on the screen in front of you so that you can see it more clearly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all right. I understood. But no further enlargement is necessary. This is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's go now to Colonel Manojlovic's partial reply. It's P1310, also dated 26 April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please enlarge a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Manojlovic in his response to General Mladic's query says that he abandoned the planned firing of the modified air-bomb because through measuring with instruments they established that two UNPROFOR points are at most 200 metres away while your own defence line was 500 metres away, and the risk to both should the weapon be fired was too great. So your own -- the safe radius of your own head of artillery is actually almost five times what you said was acceptable in your comments with regard to the Majdanska Street incident, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What chief of artillery assessed as an expert is a measure. It is something which constitutes an additional consideration to absolutely make sure that safety is achieved. Had UNPROFOR position been even further away, because of their relative vicinity, it was not justified nor would it be wise to use an air-bomb against the target being discussed here, and the target was the area of Donji Kotorac. Therefore, this is not an error, neither is it any action which would run contrary to my assertion. I maintain my efforts to explain to you that if an air-bomb exploded and somebody would be 100 metres away from the detonation site, that person would not be affected or threatened. It wouldn't be -- become a casualty, wouldn't be destroyed. It doesn't mean that this assessment was so strict if somebody would be 100 metres away we would no longer observe that. We took into consideration whether the same degree of threat would be the same for that person and for -- for the target, and this would not be a counter-argument that we should expand that radius to 200 to 850 -- 500 metres. The degree of caution expressed by this artillery expert is justified, and I acknowledge his assessment because he's the expert. There were no other intentions behind this decision except for safety.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just to go back to what you said in the earlier part of your answer, you said had the UNPROFOR position had been even further away, so even further than 200 metres, because of their relative vicinity, the use of the air-bomb would not be justified. So the question I want to ask is do you have any idea, General, how far UN Sector Sarajevo headquarters was from the impact site of the air-bomb on Majdanska Street?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It was distant enough not to be threatened. This case we are consisting which required a different approach and Majdanska are two separate matters. When it comes to Majdanska, the target needed to be fired upon because of our general jeopardy of -- the general danger that we were exposed to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, let's go over to -- more specifically to the situation in Hrasnica and the air-bomb shelling of 7 April. You said at T 32791, you talked about the size of Hrasnica and said it was covered in totality by forces that were deployed or that opened fire from within or were on furlough or there were reservists who were on standby, and you also said that the locality itself, the territory of the neighbourhood, was encumbered by the military factor and artillery assets, i.e., mortars, 120-millimetres which opened fire from that area. So when you refer to mortars which opened fire from that area, do you mean to refer to mortars in the town proper?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mortars not in the town. It wasn't a town. It was a settlement, an open ground close to certain buildings, in parks, in public parks and such areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Just in that regard, maybe we could have a look at another -- at an order drafted by you. It's D779. It was drafted by you on 27 March 1995, for an operation called Lukavac 1995. So this is about 11 days before this incident. And if we go over to the bottom of page 3 of the document in English - and with your indulgence, I'll just try and find the B/C/S page reference. I think the corresponding page is the second page in B/C/S, but at the bottom of page 3 of the English, we see information that you have about the deployment of the armaments of the 4th Motorised Brigade. You see 120-millimetre mortar platoon in the zone of Vrhovi. Now, that's not in the settlement of Hrasnica, is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And on the next page in English, same page in B/C/S, you see reference to a 105-millimetre howitzer in zone of Radeljevaca.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: An [as interpreted] 82-millimetre mortar in the zone of Vrhovi, an 82-millimetre mortar in Bijela Kosa, and a mixed mortar platoon in Kotarni Cari [phoen]. Now, none of these weapons placements are -- reflect -- or are locations in the settlement of Hrasnica at all, are they? They're actually above and behind Hrasnica centre.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, could you please return to the page where the date of the Lukavac document is listed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Intervention into the transcript. In line 19, it says "an 82-millimetre mortar." It wasn't a single piece of mortar. It was a platoon of mortars.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's okay. I've seen the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, this document also doesn't mention any facilities for weapons manufacture as being in the town or in the settlement, does it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let's be on the same page. This document was drafted in a completely different time when it was foreseen that we will have to engage our forces to carry out Operation Lukavac. However, certain changes occurred which put this document out of force, both the decision and the order and further plans of ours to carry out this activity concerning the area of Igman and the area of Treskavica. I'm familiar with this area. And when it stated where mortars are positioned, the reference is made to the region of Vrhovi, well, this is the first indication that they did not have at their disposal just one platoon of mortars and that they placed them and deployed them at Vrhovi. They had artillery pieces both at Vrhovi and within Hrasnica itself. Furthermore, these dates do not match. The change of firing position is such a simple activity and that is carried out by units, in this case our enemy. It was easy to do. Even if it weren't for the same mortars which was not the case because they had sufficient mortars to cover both Vrhovi location and Hrasnica itself. This is what I can tell you. Those two documents cannot be connected in terms of they were there and we thought they were in Hrasnica. This was not so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, same question on this as I asked you with respect to the number of command posts. You've referred to a change in firing positions. Where's the hard data for that, General? Where's the document? Because this is your own document dated only ten days beforehand.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you, what you meant when you said where is the data. Which data? What sort of data do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, you referred in your evidence in chief to documents you had in your possession. Do you have a document that establishes firing positions other than what you set out in your order of 27 May 1995 existed or that firing positions were changed from what you set out in your order of 27 May -- pardon me, 27 March.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still didn't understand, because I don't need any other document. This is an assessment, an evaluation that we had about the deployment of the enemy in order to plan the Lukavac operation. If it was planned as such and executed or was supposed to be executed, then the data was gathered and this is what we had at our disposal when we needed it. I don't know how I can add to that or to confirm the data in this situation except for what is already written there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said that between 27 March 1995 and the date of the incident on the 7th of April, Bosnian firing positions changed and moved to the town centre of Hrasnica. So let's look at another document, and it's a document dated 7 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, please. Can we have the information when this was stated? Quite the contrary. The witness said that they did have enough to have that at the same time in Hrasnica and in the hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think Dr. Karadzic is actually correct. I think I might have misunderstood the witness who said: "The change of firing position is such a simple activity and that's carried out by units, in this case our enemy. Even if it weren't for the same mortars which was not the case because they had sufficient mortars to cover both Vrhovi location and Hrasnica itself." So, yes, I apologise. My misunderstanding of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I'd still like to go to the document dated 7 April 1995, and it's P5943, and it's a VRS Main Staff report to Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please zoom in on the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe one more magnification for the general, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if you go over in this document and the numbering is difficult in the B/C/S. Let me just see if I can scan it. I want to go over to paragraph 6, and its kind of jammed together on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that paragraph, the number 6, anywhere. Could you perhaps tell me how the text begins?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's on --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Mm-hmm, okay. [Interpretation] I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's on B/C/S page 3 and it's paragraph 3 I'm after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies. And English page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this paragraph says at 6.00 a.m. that morning, the enemy opened up heavy fire from Gradina, Igman, and Lasica. So would you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- agree with me that all these locations are up in the hills or in the case of Lasica that's right next to the confrontation line by the Famos factory?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct, yes. Lasica is in the town, in the settlement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this document says that -- pardon me. So then the origin of fire for the launching or in response to which this 250 kilo air-bomb was launched, and that's at sub-heading B, under paragraph 3, actually was outside of the settlement centre, whereas the bomb was launched in the town centre, General. The fire, according to this report that the bomb responded to actually had nothing to do with ABiH activity from Hrasnica centre at all. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that wasn't like that. You didn't give me an opportunity to say what the circumstances were and what the situation was in Hrasnica. I must give an explanation that the commander of the Ilidza Brigade had for a long time insisted that a solution be found how to prevent the mortar and artillery fire from the Hrasnica section. The Ilidza area and the entire part from Stojcevci across the basins, the pools, the institute, the spas, and the villas were threatened by this fire coming from Hrasnica. He didn't start to show it to me and to look for a solution. For example, if there was fire on the 7th, he didn't ask for it on the 5th, but it would be a few days before. I had to be in the situation, because from where I was, I couldn't see Hrasnica from Ilidza. So in order to have confirmation of what was actually happening there and whether that corresponded to what the commander was saying. There was an area called Siljak. It was above Ilidza, and these are already the slopes of Mount Igman. That is where -- from where we could see the force that was inside and the assets, how they were deployed. The basic thing is that there were mortars and firing positions there deployed in the same way as they were at Vrhovi. Let me add this as well: The image and noting the indicators was at the same time when there was firing. It just happened by chance. They weren't aware that somebody was monitoring what they were doing in that particular time. So I ascertained that there was fire in that area, and I could then see how much under threat the commander and his sector was by that fire. And on the basis of that, I had to agree with him to neutralise that fire. I can tell you later or I can tell you right now how things went on from there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 5 in the transcript, the witness was misunderstood. He didn't say that it would be a few days before. He said "even," it would be even more than a few days earlier. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the timing of the fire was not in -- the timing of the fire of the air-bomb was not in any way proximate in time to the mortar fire you've referred to.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why that would be so and where the misunderstanding comes from. I gave an explanation as to what was seen at another time, but this fire continued, and somehow now we cannot come to the conclusion that you would like to draw that since it happened on the 7th that would be when actually nobody was firing at all. There would not have been any fire on the 7th either -- or, rather, on the 6th, is that right? If there had been no fire before that at some point, this is what happened then, that at some point the air-bomb was used. I hope that you understood that nothing was left to chance because that Hrasnica was too active and it's forces as well, that we were firing whenever we felt like it. We had a lot of patience as well as attempted to thwart it in a different way than it would be done, but in this case they weren't pardoning themselves at all, never mind us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your evidence is this air-bomb was fired to neutralise a mortar; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not mortar but mortars. Artillery weapons. Actually, in this case there were four of them. I mean, it wasn't a question of one mortar. You wouldn't retaliate for one mortar.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, still on the subject of this incident, you also in your evidence at 32796 said that the Aleksa Santic school was a place where they made hand grenades and rifle grenades in Hrasnica. Did you know that a Serb resident of Hrasnica actually came to testify in Dr. Karadzic's defence and specifically said that there was no production going on in the school and the only thing going on was melting in the gym and the manufacturing process took place somewhere else? And he said that at transcript page 32087.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was based on data that I was given by certain people. That connection, movements, contacts, they were not so exclusive so that somebody from Hrasnica would not be able to come to provide information about what was going on in Ilidza and that this data could then be offered up. I do acknowledge the testimony of that witness, but as far as he's concerned, if he had better information at disposal, then -- our information also was grounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, if it was, where were the mortars positioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the mortars were located in open areas, in areas that could be described as parks or locations where there were no buildings. They were next to buildings, in the vicinity of buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's just -- and did you receive information that the mortars had been neutralised?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's understand the following first: When the decision was given to use the air-bomb, the order was sent to the hands of Colonel Radovcic [phoen], and in the order it stated, which usually is there, it's a rule that has to be applied, that the air-bomb or some other asset, but the air-bomb in this case has to be prepared. It has to be ready to act. Once it's prepared, when the information is confirmed that the asset is prepared, the information would reach me, then there would be a couple of checks so that we make sure that it's no longer technical preparedness but that we would need to check what the situation was in the location where the asset is supposed to be fired, and then the information was that the target was still visible, the target was still active, and that the asset can be fired, and all of that would then stop at this check and making sure that everything was as it is, and then we would wait for my order for the fire to go ahead. As for some more immediate indicators, then I would perhaps receive further such information or data about the situation as it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, General, with respect, the evidence that we've discussed today suggest that it would be impossible to pinpoint a target with these air-bombs. You've said that the air-bombs weren't fired over Serb residential areas because they might land on them. Your chief of artillery wouldn't fire air-bombs on a target within 500 metres of your own forces because of the risk that the bomb might land on them, and I would suggest to you, General, that whether or not the target was visible, it was impossible to pinpoint something like that with this weapon without risk of civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the assessment isn't made in the way as to guarantee that there would be absolutely no civilian casualties. The risk is calculated on the basis of an estimation of possible collateral damage compared to the option of halting these assets that were endangering us. I don't know if you can see in view of the locality the area. Those same assets are so easily fired at Vojkovici without any restraint at Grlica and at parts over there around the Famos factory, and in the same way they fired at Ilidza. These are not two opposite sides. So it was simple to direct fire. These assets, these weapons from Hrasnica were not threatening just a sector of the front but a broad sweep of the area for manoeuvring an action. So the calculations had to take into account what had to be done so that the civilian population would not suffer if the target was engaged. Calculations were made so that the target would be destroyed without destroying a large number of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, your own orders explicitly refer to the probability of a miss when you used these air-bombs. Let's have a look at P1309. It's your order dated 21 April, 1995, for the operation called Talas. Talas 1, in fact. And in both languages, we can go over to page 2, paragraph 2. This orders -- this is your order. It says: "Proceed forthwith to prepare launchers to make sure that four to six aerial bombs can be launched simultaneously against the designated target, the condition being that they must hit the target, which means that the provisions have to be made for more bombs so that in the event of a miss, the next projectile lands on the target." General, you actually had an expectation that these bombs wouldn't hit the target as evidenced by this order and you still fired them against Hrasnica and other areas of Sarajevo where civilians were found?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent question, and you will get my answer. It's not a question here of firing. It's -- it's -- we're talking about firing at a target here. It's a question of terminology.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In the B/C/S, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not an artillery battery but a launcher. So immediately prepare a launcher and ensure that the selected target is hit by four to six air-bombs on condition that they hit the target. It cannot be permitted that the crew -- well, not the crew but the commanding officer controlling the assets prepares to such an extent and makes such a calculation that they -- the target would be hit. This is one thing. Secondly, the commander -- and here I officially note that the commander cannot know everything, and my people who understand this much better said to me immediately that you cannot fire more than one air-bomb at a time because the firing is followed by preparation, namely once one is fired and it does not hit the target, then a lot of time is required, and I think they told me that it's about two hours, to prepare a new one. The two hours would imply completely revealing the asset, which is quite large, and it would be out of the question to keep it where it was, because then it would be exposed to enemy fire. So in essence, we did not change the contents of the regulations, but we nuanced and detailed so that everything would come down to the use of one air-bomb calculated in such a manner that it's to the target. Contrary to that, the professional controlling the fire and overseeing the precision of fire would not even proceed to firing point unless he could rely on this precision. So he tried to stick to what was there as closely as possible without changing the rules and the text of the content.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see it's 2.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll continue tomorrow, but before we adjourn, I briefly have two matters, Mr. Tieger. Would you like to respond to the Defence motion for a request Mr. Krstic's lawyer to be present in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think an e-mail was just sent on that, Mr. President, and I won't pre-empt the contents, but I believe we don't have a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And do you have any observation about the Defence motion to -- Defence response to your motion to exclude the evidence of Snezana Kovac in which the Defence wants to tender those remaining relevant paragraphs pursuant to Rule 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On that one I think I'm behind the curve and I'll have to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if we could hear your response as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As soon as possible, of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is now adjourned. We will begin -- we'll resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 5th day of February, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.46 p.m.,
